records.claim: LangGraph exhibits five recurring production failure patterns: unbounded checkpoint state causing memory exhaustion; recursive loops exceeding the default recursion limit with cryptic termination; silent last-write-wins data loss from concurrent branch updates; checkpointer backend connection exhaustion at concurrency; and human-in-the-loop interrupt state becoming unresumable after a deployment restart.
records.source_title: LangGraph in production: five failure patterns
records.retrieved_evidence: "Checkpoint state growing unbounded when a graph's message history is persisted without pruning, leading to memory exhaustion on long-running conversational agents; recursive agent loops exceeding LangGraph's default recursion limit and terminating mid-task with a cryptic error instead of a graceful fallback; concurrent state updates from parallel graph branches producing silent last-write-wins data loss when the reducer function isn't configured... checkpointer backend connection exhaustion under concurrent agent sessions... and human-in-the-loop interrupt state becoming unresumable after a deployment restart."
records.credibility: Independent consultancy failure-pattern writeup, specific and mechanism-level; page opened and excerpt verified 2026-10-24

records.claim: CrewAI exhibits five recurring production failure patterns: silent context truncation in task handoffs; hierarchical crews stalling on unregistered worker agents; tool-calling agents looping indefinitely (no circuit breaker in default retry); cost/latency multiplying as sequential crews grow; and memory configuration inconsistency causing agents to contradict earlier-established facts.
records.source_title: CrewAI in production: five failure patterns
records.retrieved_evidence: "Task output handoffs between agents silently truncating context when the crew's process mode passes only the final task output instead of full intermediate reasoning, hierarchical crews stalling when the manager agent's delegation tool calls a worker agent that isn't correctly registered... tool-calling agents looping indefinitely on a failing tool because the default retry behaviour has no circuit breaker, cost and latency multiplying unexpectedly when a sequential crew's agent count grows... and memory configuration inconsistency... causing agents to contradict earlier-established facts within the same run."
records.credibility: Independent consultancy failure-pattern writeup; page opened and excerpt verified 2026-10-24

records.claim: In CrewAI, task routing is opaque in hierarchical mode (the manager's routing decision is inside an LLM call and cannot be unit-tested) while sequential mode is explicit but too inflexible for conditional branching.
records.source_title: Where CrewAI Broke in Two Systems I Migrated
records.retrieved_evidence: "The production problem is that hierarchical routing did not give me an explicit, inspectable decision, while sequential routing was explicit but too inflexible for conditional branches. In hierarchical mode, the manager's routing decision is inside an LLM call. I could not write a unit test that asserts 'given this task, route to...'"
records.credibility: First-hand practitioner account of two production migrations; mechanism-specific

records.claim: CrewAI is optimized for getting agent systems moving quickly, not for being the production platform around long-running enterprise work; its production gaps (capacity, process failure, signals) all appear at once and none are visible in the demo.
records.source_title: CrewAI Gets You to the Demo. Then What?
records.retrieved_evidence: "The core distinction still holds: it is optimized for getting agent systems moving quickly, not for becoming the production platform around long-running enterprise work. Where the Gap Opens The problems start when you need the system to keep working under real production conditions... they all show up at once, and none of them are visible in the demo. Capacity, process failure, signals — the durability surface."
records.credibility: Practitioner essay (enterprise software background); critique direction consistent with E19/E20 and acknowledged in part by the vendor itself (E16)

records.claim: LangGraph, CrewAI, and Google ADK all offer checkpointing that 'falls far short of durable execution' — they save state but leave failure detection, automatic recovery, and duplicate prevention entirely to the user.
records.source_title: Still Not Durable: How Microsoft Agent Framework and Strands Agents Repeat the Same Mistakes
records.retrieved_evidence: "In the first part of this series, I walked through how LangGraph, CrewAI, and Google ADK all offer checkpointing and resumability features that fall far short of durable execution. The core problem: they save state, but leave failure detection, automatic recovery, and duplicate prevention entirely to you."
records.credibility: Third-party infrastructure vendor with a commercial interest in durable execution (Diagrid sells related tooling) — noted, but the analysis is source-code-inspected and mechanism-specific

records.claim: In Microsoft Agent Framework, resume is entirely manual: restore_from_checkpoint requires an explicit checkpoint_id, with no supervisor, scheduler, automatic restart, heartbeat, lease mechanism, or watchdog — at hundreds of concurrent workflows the entire detection-and-retry infrastructure must be built by the user.
records.source_title: Still Not Durable: How Microsoft Agent Framework and Strands Agents Repeat the Same Mistakes
records.retrieved_evidence: "Resume is entirely manual. Looking at the actual source code, the restore_from_checkpoint method in the Runner class requires the caller to provide an explicit checkpoint_id. There is no supervisor, no scheduler, no automatic restart... At scale — hundreds of concurrent workflows — you need to build the entire detection-and-retry infrastructure yourself. No automatic failure detection. The workflow runner has no heartbeat, no lease mechanism, no watchdog."
records.credibility: Source-code-inspected analysis by an infrastructure vendor (commercial interest noted, as E22)

records.claim: The OpenAI Agents SDK in production needs a runtime the SDK does not provide: teams wrap it in FastAPI, workers, and Kubernetes and add retries, but durable execution for long-running multi-step runs (e.g., runs paused awaiting approval) remains their responsibility.
records.source_title: OpenAI Agents are great. Production still needs a runtime.
records.retrieved_evidence: "Most teams get further than that. They wrap it in FastAPI. They run it in a worker. They put it on Kubernetes. They add retries around the obvious network calls... That gets you a long way. It does not quite give you a runtime. A support run has already looked up order ORD-1007, checked the shipping policy, and drafted most of the answer. Then it reaches a sensitive action: issue a refund, cancel a shipment..."
records.credibility: ZenML sells an agent runtime (Kitaru) — commercial interest in this exact claim; direction is consistent with E22/E23 (independent durability analyses)

records.claim: The OpenAI Agents SDK carries a model lock-in surface: it is designed around the OpenAI Chat Completions/Responses APIs, and switching providers requires work (built-in LiteLLM/Any-LLM adapter integration points arrived only around mid-2025).
records.source_title: OpenAI Agents SDK: Simple to Start, Easy to Outgrow?
records.retrieved_evidence: "Model lock-in. The SDK is designed around the OpenAI Chat Completions API and, increasingly, the newer Responses API. Switching to a different model provider — Anthropic, Google, a self-hosted Mistral — requires work. As of mid-2025 the SDK added built-in provider integration points (including beta LiteLLM and Any-LLM adapters)..."
records.credibility: Independent consultancy review; page opened and excerpt verified 2026-10-24

records.claim: Google ADK's 1.0 release broke existing users' code despite being announced as production-ready, with GitHub issues full of similar reports and advice to roll back; multi-agent deployments show probabilistic stability concerns.

records.retrieved_evidence: "At Google I/O they announced 1.0—supposed to be production-ready. It wasn't. I upgraded and my code broke. GitHub issues were full of similar reports, people told to roll back... They timed the release for the conference, but claimed production readiness when it wasn't true." Other developers noted: "It has to get more stable. When we build more agents in one system, discrepancies appear, but it's probabilistic, may or may not happen."

records.claim: Google's own Agent Runtime documentation records a cold-start latency of approximately 4.7 seconds at min_instances=1 under 300 concurrent requests (vs ~0.4s warm), a scale cost the operator must mitigate with instance settings.

gaps.description: No independent source publishes a trailing-12-months combined adoption ranking (downloads + contributors + stars + production use). The ranking in this run is constructed from primary registry/repository data (E7-E13) plus independent dated snapshots (E1-E3); no new search was planned for RQ3 (per the approved plan).

Mastra (29.0K stars, active) excluded from the ranking: GitHub API reports license NOASSERTION (E14) and the LICENSE file was not read to resolve recognized-OSS status — verification not attempted within this run.

OpenClaw shows 17% adoption in the Stack Overflow April 2026 pulse (E4) but was not classified: personal-assistant gateway vs agent-framework boundary unresolved; excluded from the code-framework ranking.

Two promising sources were rejected because full pages could not be retrieved (Medium/towards.ai LangGraph checkpointing postmortem — anti-bot wall, 60 chars returned; vdf.ai 2026-10-06 ten-framework roundup — fetch failure). Per evidence-recording rules, search snippets were not recorded as evidence. vdf.ai also reportedly covers 'what happened to AutoGen' — corroborating E6 if ever retrieved.

Pydantic AI (5.4M downloads/mo, 20.8K stars — E13) sits at the top-5/6 boundary; no independent scale-breakdown account for it surfaced in the planned RQ4 queries (which targeted the top-5). If stage 03 or the report ranks it top-5, its RQ4 independence obligation is unmet and must be reported as a gap.
